profile.name: Kalinka
profile.tagline: A spirited Russian concert folk dance set to Ivan Larionov's iconic 1860 song.
profile.insight: Written in 1860 by Ivan Larionov as theatrical entertainment, this snowball-tree song evolved into a frenetic stage dance and global Russian icon.
profile.profile: Kalinka is a Russian concert folk dance and song written in 1860 by composer and folklorist Ivan Larionov in Saratov. The performance features a speedy tempo that increases with each iteration of the refrain, celebrating the snowball tree. Over the decades, it transitioned from theatrical entertainment into a globally recognized staple of Russian folk performance, famously popularized by the Alexandrov Ensemble.
profile.profile_long: Kalinka is a traditional Russian song and concert folk dance that originated in 1860. Written by the composer and folklorist Ivan Larionov, it was first performed in Saratov as part of a theatrical entertainment piece he composed, soon entering the repertoire of folk choral groups. The song's refrain refers to the kalinka, which is the snowball tree (Viburnum opulus), with lyrics containing layered metaphors relating to love, youth, and nature. Performers and dancers often engage in a frenetic celebration of singing and dancing as the music progresses. Since the end of World War II, the song and its associated performance traditions have been heavily popularized by the Alexandrov Ensemble, the official army choir group of the Russian Armed Forces. Over time, Kalinka has transcended its theatrical origins to become a famous symbol of Russian folk culture worldwide, appearing extensively in global media, international ceremonies, and concert repertoires.

sections.origins_and_history: Kalinka was written in 1860 by Ivan Larionov in Saratov as part of a theatrical work. It was subsequently added to folk choral repertoires and gained major international prominence after World War II through the Alexandrov Ensemble.
sections.music_and_instruments: The music features a speedy tempo and light-hearted lyrics. The main refrain increases in tempo each time it is sung. Key vocalists and groups include the Alexandrov Ensemble, Evgeny Belyaev, and Pyotr Tverdokhlebov.
sections.occasions_and_meaning: The song's refrain refers to the kalinka (snowball tree, Viburnum opulus), which symbolizes love, youth, and passion in traditional Slavic culture. Singers and dancers often enter into a frantic celebration during performances.
sections.notable_figures: Ivan Larionov (composer), Evgeny Belyaev, Pyotr Tverdokhlebov, Viktor Nikitin, Boris Alexandrovich Alexandrov, and Aida Garifullina.
sections.lineage: Classified as a Russian concert folk dance and folk-style song originating in the mid-19th century.

music_profile.rhythm_pattern: Speedy tempo with an increasing tempo during the main refrain each time it is sung.
music_profile.vocal_style: Choir and operatic tenor soloists (such as the Alexandrov Ensemble and Evgeny Belyaev)
music_profile.musical_form: Song and refrain structure with a progressive accelerando
music_profile.sound_description: A rapid, accelerating choral and instrumental arrangement that shifts from gentle poetic verses to a frenetic, high-tempo refrain.
